title_tag: AI-to-Human Handoff: When an AI Agent Should Hand Off
meta_description: When should an AI agent hand off to a human? Six triggers for an AI-to-human handoff, what the person needs, and the 15-minute rule in California.
h1: AI-to-human handoff: when should an AI agent hand off to a human?
answer_first: An AI agent should hand off to a human when the customer asks for one, when the next step crosses a limit you set or needs judgment, when the answer is not in your own sources, or when the agent has failed twice on the same request. A good AI-to-human handoff gives the person the whole conversation and a record of what the agent already did, so the customer never has to start over.
body_html:
An AI agent should hand off to a human when the customer asks for one, when the next step crosses a limit you set or needs judgment, when the answer is not in your own sources, or when the agent has failed twice on the same request. A good AI-to-human handoff gives the person the whole conversation and a record of what the agent already did, so the customer never has to start over.

The route to a person decides how customers feel about the agent. In Gartner's survey of 5,728 customers, 64% said they would prefer companies did not use AI for customer service, and the top worry was that AI would make it harder to reach a person (Gartner, July 2024).

What should trigger an AI-to-human handoff?

Write escalation triggers as rules the agent checks on every turn. Six cover most businesses:

TriggerExampleWhat the agent does
The customer asks for a person"Can I talk to someone?", "agent", pressing 0Hands off at once, with no retry
A limit is crossedA refund above your approval limit, a discount outside policyAsks the named approver, or hands off
No source for the answerThe policy page is silent, or two pages disagreeHands off instead of guessing
Repeated failureThe customer asks the same thing twice, or an action fails twiceStops the loop and hands off
An action is not confirmedThe booking or refund never shows up in your systemSays so, and hands off
A sensitive topicA complaint, a legal threat, a safety issue, a billing disputeHands off with the reason flagged

Frustration and confidence scores can add early warnings, but a request for a person should never wait on a score. Treat it as a hard rule, in any wording and on any channel.

A limit is not always a full handoff. If a refund only needs a manager's yes, the agent can ask for that approval and finish the task itself. Hand over the conversation when the customer needs to talk to someone.

What should the person receive?

A transcript is not enough. The person taking over should be able to reply well in their first message, which means the handoff carries:

  • who the customer is, matched to one record;
  • the request in one sentence, with the full history from every channel;
  • each action the agent took, and whether your system confirmed it;
  • why the agent stopped, and the decision it needs;
  • what the customer was told about timing.

On the customer's side, the agent should say that a person is coming and roughly when. Once a person joins, the agent stays quiet in that conversation. When the person is done, the agent can pick up the remaining tasks, with the decision on record.

How fast does a person need to respond?

California now puts a number on it. Governor Newsom signed AB 1609, the Right to Human Customer Service Act, on September 28, 2026 (Office of the Governor). According to the Senate Judiciary Committee analysis, it applies to businesses with more than $500 million in annual revenue, and requires them to:

  • offer a clear way to ask for a person on every customer service channel, chatbots and phone lines included, during business hours;
  • make a good-faith effort to connect the customer within 15 minutes, or offer a specific appointment within one business day;
  • tell customers when they are talking to a chatbot.

The San Francisco Standard reports that the rules start next year. This is not legal advice, so check the final text with counsel. Smaller businesses are not covered, but the numbers are a sensible target anyway. In practice that means a named owner for every handoff, a queue someone actually watches, and a specific callback time to offer when nobody is free.

Frequently asked questions

Is a high handoff rate a bad sign?

Not on its own. Track the handoff rate together with the reason for each handoff. A rising share of "no source" handoffs points to gaps in your documents, which you can fix. If you push the rate down by making people harder to reach, customers notice.

What if nobody is available to take the handoff?

The agent should say so plainly, offer a specific callback time or the next opening, and record the promise as a task with an owner. A vague "someone will get back to you" with no owner is how requests get dropped.

Next steps

Write your six triggers down before you launch an agent, along with who owns each one. An AI-to-human handoff only works if someone is on the other end.
